messages.subject: Re: Sleep efficiency - operationalization
messages.body_plain:
Hi, the reason of asking about this point is because one reviewer is asking for more details about the operationalization of sleep efficiency.
I went through your paper (van Hees, V. T., Sabia, S., Anderson, K. N., Denton, S. J., Oliver, J., Catt, M., . . . Singh-Manoux, A. (2015). A Novel, Open Access Method to Assess Sleep Duration Using a Wrist-Worn Accelerometer. PLoS One, 10(11). doi:ARTN e0142533
10.1371/journal.pone.0142533), but it looks like you did not use this information.

It looks like people are discussing more about the details.
Reed, D. L., & Sacco, W. P. (2016). Measuring Sleep Efficiency: What Should the Denominator Be? J Clin Sleep Med, 12(2), 263-266. doi:10.5664/jcsm.5498

Regards.

Guillermo

messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] Re: Sleep efficiency - operationalization
messages.body_plain:
Hi, That depends on the type of questionnaire you used. The formal definition of sleep efficiency is calculated relative to the window between intention to fall asleep and waking up in the morning. As we do not always have this window our revised definition becomes the ration of time slept within the sleep period time. This is not because I disagree with the convention, but because there is no other way to calculate it. Users should just be careful with interpretation as both approaches are obviously not compatible. If your questionnaire asks about time of intention to fall asleep then your sleep efficiency results should be compatible with the conventional approach. Best wishes, Vincent

The explanation I gave on Friday was specific to part 4. Part 5 currently uses the Sleep period time window as denominator for its sleep efficiency estimate, so that is not consistent with the convention.
For as far as I know, the sleep variables from part 5 have not been used in publications yet.

Regards, Vincent

messages.body_plain:
Hi Tom,

I've been encountering the same problem several times and now I think I've found a solution (fingers crossed...): I changed the separator of the csv file from semicolon to comma (; -> ,). I've made the csv-files in Excel, and this is not the first time the country-specific settings in Excel have caused a headache.

I don't know if you still have this problem, but as I've found this forum very helpful in other aspects, I just wanted to post this. Maybe it'll help others.

Best wishes,
Anna

messages.subject: GGIR version 1.5-18
messages.body_plain:
Dear GGIR users,

GGIR version 1.5-18 is now online, the key updates are:

1. Improved handling of day saving time (DST) in g.part3 and g.part4.
In the older version DST was accounted for in part 2, but not in the
sleep parameter estimates produced with part 4.

2. Sleep period time window detection algorithm HDCZA is now the
default algorithm to use, when a sleeplog is used and a diary entry is
missing for a particular night. Following my recent work it seems that
HDCZA is far superior than L5+/-6hr, so I think it is justified to
make HDCZA the default fall back option
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/early/2018/02/01/257972.

3. pdf generation in part 3 is now optional (argument do.part3.pdf),
this may be useful for slightly speeding up data processing as it
takes a few second to generate the pdf file, which can accumulate if
your process a lot of files.

The first two changes will affect your sleep parameter estimates for
measurements in which the sleep window overlapped with DST, so please
be mindful that your results may not be consistent with past results.

Best wishes,
Vincent

messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] Re: GGIR version 1.5-18
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jairo,

Yes, if no sleep diary data is available in a study I would recommend
using argument def.noc.sleep = 1, which activates the new HDZCA
algorithm.

It may be worth highlighting that neither of the methods has been
described or 'validated' in a peer reviewed journal article yet. The
article https://www.biorxiv.org/content/early/2018/02/01/257972 is
currently under review at a journal.
I added the L5+/-6 hours algorithm to GGIR in 2015 as a quick approach
to facilitate ongoing methodological research.

Best,
Vincent

messages.subject: Re: GGIR version 1.5-18
messages.body_plain:
Just to clarify with regard to point 1 in my e-mail previous e-mail.

The day saving time has always been correctly accounted for in GGIR.
The only thing that was wrong in previous versions of GGIR and is now
corrected are the sleep parameter estimates derived from the two
nights in the year when the time changes forward or backward.
The code naively calculated the difference between sleep onset and
waking up time, without considering the extra hour or the skipped
hour.

Sorry for my earlier message was not clear.

Best wishes,
Vincent
